M<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> (d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>), with x<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub>/(0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b)
A<sub>st</sub> = (0.5 f<sub>ck</sub>/f<sub>y</sub>)[1 − √(1 − 4.6 M<sub>u</sub>/(f<sub>ck</sub> b d²))] b d
0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u,max</sub> (d − 0.42 x<sub>u,max</sub>) = 0.148, 0.138, 0.133 f<sub>ck</sub> b d²

From ε<sub>sc</sub> = 0.0035(x<sub>u,max</sub> − d′)/x<sub>u,max</sub> on the bar's curve; Fe415: 355, 353, 342, 329 N/mm² for d′/d = 0.05 to 0.20
T-beam L<sub>0</sub>/6 + b<sub>w</sub> + 6Df; L-beam L<sub>0</sub>/12 + b<sub>w</sub> + 3Df; not more than the spacing limit

p<sub>t</sub> = 50 (f<sub>ck</sub>/f<sub>y</sub>)[1 − √(1 − 4.6 (M<sub>u</sub>/bd²)/f<sub>ck</sub>)], tabulated in SP 16 against M<sub>u</sub>/bd²
span/250 final; span/350 or 20 mm after partitions
L/d ≤ (7, 20 or 26) × k<sub>t</sub> × k<sub>c</sub> × k<sub>f</sub>; × 10/span over 10 m
0.3 mm general, 0.2 mm exposed, 0.1 mm aggressive; Annex F formula w<sub>cr</sub> = 3acr ε<sub>m</sub>/[1 + 2(a<sub>cr</sub> − C<sub>min</sub>)/(D − x)]
m = E<sub>s</sub>/E<sub>c</sub> with E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√f<sub>ck</sub> (short term); m = 280/(3σcbc) for working stress
M<sub>cr</sub> = f<sub>cr</sub> I/y<sub>t</sub> with f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub>; Annex C uses the gross section
b x²/2 = m A<sub>st</sub> (d − x); I<sub>cr</sub> = b x³/3 + m A<sub>st</sub> (d − x)²

takeaways: At collapse a beam is a couple: the concrete block 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> at 0.42 x<sub>u</sub> from the top, and the steel 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub>; C = T gives x<sub>u</sub> and the couple gives M<sub>u</sub>.
The neutral axis may not go below x<sub>u,max</sub> (0.53d, 0.48d, 0.46d), so a singly reinforced section stops at M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.148, 0.138 or 0.133 f<sub>ck</sub> b d².
A section with A<sub>st</sub> above A<sub>st,lim</sub> is over-reinforced: it crushes suddenly, and the code credits only M<sub>u,lim</sub> however much steel it has.

Above M<sub>u,lim</sub>, compression steel and an equal force of extra tension steel carry the excess; for Fe415 and Fe500 the compression steel stress comes from the curved design diagram (about 353 N/mm² for Fe415), not 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>.

A monolithic slab makes a T or L beam: find b<sub>f</sub> from the code, test whether the flange can balance the steel, and use 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub> on the overhangs with y<sub>f</sub> when the neutral axis is in the web.
SP 16 tables are the same equations solved in advance: enter with M<sub>u</sub>/bd², read p<sub>t</sub> (and p<sub>c</sub> for doubly reinforced sections).

Serviceability is checked at service loads: L/d against 20 × k<sub>t</sub> × k<sub>c</sub> × k<sub>f</sub> for deflection, bar spacing and cover for cracks, and the Annex F formula when a crack width is needed.
The transformed section links the two states: (m − 1)A<sub>st</sub> before cracking gives M<sub>cr</sub>, m A<sub>st</sub> after cracking gives the service stresses and the stiffness for deflection.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the analysis and design of flanged beams with the neutral axis both in the flange and in the web, the use of design aids for flexure, and serviceability checks for deflection and cracking; singly and doubly reinforced rectangular sections come up as design problems with numbers. Show every step: M<sub>u,lim</sub> first, then x<sub>u</sub>, then the steel, then the code limits.

bank.q: State the assumptions of IS 456 for the limit state of collapse in flexure. Derive the stress block parameters 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub> and 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>, and the values of x<sub>u,max</sub>/d for Fe250, Fe415 and Fe500.
outline: Six assumptions of clause 38.1
Parabola-rectangle diagram: peak 0.446 f<sub>ck</sub>, parabola up to strain 0.002, flat to 0.0035
Area of the diagram gives 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub>; its centroid gives 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>
Limiting steel strain 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub> + 0.002 and the strain diagram give x<sub>u,max</sub>/d
answer: Assumptions (IS 456 clause 38.1): (a) plane sections remain plane, so strain is linear with depth; (b) the maximum compressive strain in concrete is 0.0035; (c) concrete stress follows the design parabola-rectangle curve with a peak of 0.67 f<sub>ck</sub>/1.5 = 0.446 f<sub>ck</sub>; (d) the tensile strength of concrete is ignored; (e) steel stress is taken from its design stress-strain curve with γm = 1.15, so the design yield stress is 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>; (f) at collapse the tension steel strain is not less than 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub> + 0.002.

Stress over the depth x<sub>u</sub>. The strain is 0.0035 at the top and zero at the neutral axis. The parabola ends where the strain is 0.002, that is at a distance (0.002/0.0035) x<sub>u</sub> = 4/7 x<sub>u</sub> above the neutral axis. So the top 3/7 x<sub>u</sub> carries a constant 0.446 f<sub>ck</sub>, and the lower 4/7 x<sub>u</sub> carries a parabola rising from zero to 0.446 f<sub>ck</sub>.

answer.text: Area of the stress diagram per unit width (the compression force):
answer.pre:
rectangle: 0.446 f<sub>ck</sub> × (3/7) x<sub>u</sub>        = 0.1911 f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub>
parabola:  (2/3) × 0.446 f<sub>ck</sub> × (4/7) x<sub>u</sub> = 0.1699 f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub>
total:     0.3610 f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub>  ≈ 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub>
C = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub>

answer.text: Position of the force, measured from the top fibre. The rectangle's centroid is at 3/14 x<sub>u</sub> = 0.2143 x<sub>u</sub>. The parabola's centroid is 5/8 of its height above the neutral axis: 5/8 × 4/7 x<sub>u</sub> = 0.357 x<sub>u</sub> above it, that is 0.643 x<sub>u</sub> below the top.

answer: Limiting depth. At the balanced point the top is at 0.0035 and the steel at ε<sub>s,lim</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub> + 0.002. Similar triangles give x<sub>u,max</sub>/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + ε<sub>s,lim</sub>) = 0.0035/(0.0055 + 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub>).

Use of the results: M<sub>u</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> (d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>) = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> (d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>), and with x<sub>u</sub> = x<sub>u,max</sub> the limiting moment is M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.148, 0.138 or 0.133 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² for the three grades.
Check: the computed factors 0.3610 and 0.416 round to the code's 0.36 and 0.42, and the three ratios round to the values in the note to clause 38.1.

bank.q: Explain balanced, under-reinforced and over-reinforced sections with strain diagrams and state the failure mode of each. For a beam 250 mm wide with d = 450 mm in M25 and Fe415, classify the section and find its moment of resistance for A<sub>st</sub> = 1000 mm² and A<sub>st</sub> = 1600 mm².
outline: Strain diagram pivoting on 0.0035 at the top
Three cases by x<sub>u</sub> against x<sub>u,max</sub>; ductile versus brittle failure
A<sub>st,lim</sub> and p<sub>t,lim</sub> for the grades
A<sub>st</sub> = 1000 mm²: under-reinforced, M<sub>u</sub> from the couple
A<sub>st</sub> = 1600 mm²: over-reinforced, M<sub>u</sub> limited to M<sub>u,lim</sub>
answer: At collapse the strain diagram is a straight line from 0.0035 (compression) at the top to ε<sub>s</sub> at the steel. Its zero is the neutral axis at depth x<sub>u</sub>. A shallow x<sub>u</sub> gives a large steel strain; a deep x<sub>u</sub> gives a small one: ε<sub>s</sub> = 0.0035(d − x<sub>u</sub>)/x<sub>u</sub>.

Under-reinforced (x<sub>u</sub> < x<sub>u,max</sub>): the steel reaches ε<sub>s,lim</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>/E<sub>s</sub> + 0.002 first and keeps stretching at 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> while the concrete has not crushed. The beam deflects and cracks widely before the concrete finally crushes: a ductile failure with warning. This is what design aims for.
Balanced (x<sub>u</sub> = x<sub>u,max</sub>): the steel reaches ε<sub>s,lim</sub> at the moment the concrete reaches 0.0035. It is the boundary between the two modes, with moment M<sub>u,lim</sub>.

Over-reinforced (x<sub>u</sub> > x<sub>u,max</sub>): the concrete crushes while the steel is still below its full design stress. Failure is sudden and explosive, with little deflection. IS 456 does not allow it; when an existing section is over-reinforced, its moment of resistance is limited to M<sub>u,lim</sub>.

answer.text: Limits for b = 250 mm, d = 450 mm, M25, Fe415:

answer.pre:
first estimate x<sub>u</sub> = 361.05 × 1600 / 2250 = 256.7 mm  > 216 mm  → over-reinforced
code moment of resistance = M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 174.6 kN·m
(strain compatibility gives x<sub>u</sub> = 250.5 mm, f<sub>s</sub> = 352.3 N/mm², true collapse moment 194.3 kN·m)

answer: Comment: 60 % more steel (1600 against 1000 mm²) raises the credited moment only from 138.1 to 174.6 kN·m, and anything above 1346 mm² is wasted because the code stops at M<sub>u,lim</sub>. If 194 kN·m were needed, the section should be made deeper or doubly reinforced so that it stays ductile.
Check: 1000 < 1346.1 < 1600 mm², consistent with the two x<sub>u</sub> values lying either side of 216 mm.

bank.q: Explain why only part of a slab acts as the flange of a T-beam, and state the IS 456 rules for effective flange width. A continuous floor beam of span 7.5 m has a web 300 mm wide and a slab 125 mm thick, with beams at 3.5 m centres. Find b<sub>f</sub> for an interior T-beam, an edge L-beam and an isolated T-beam whose actual flange is 1200 mm wide.
outline: Monolithic slab acts as compression flange in sagging moment
Shear lag: stress falls away from the web
T, L and isolated formulas and the spacing limit
L<sub>0</sub> for a continuous beam about 0.7 × span
Numbers: 1925, 1112.5 and 927 mm; hogging zones are rectangles
answer: In sagging bending the top of the beam is in compression, and the slab cast with it shares that compression. The force reaches the slab through shear at the slab-web junction, so the slab next to the web is strained almost as much as the web, but farther away the compression lags behind. This uneven distribution is called shear lag. Instead of integrating it, IS 456 uses an effective width b<sub>f</sub> over which a uniform stress gives the same force.

The flange works only in compression. Over the supports of a continuous beam the moment is hogging, the slab is in tension and cracks, and the section is designed as a rectangle of the web width b<sub>w</sub>.

answer.text: IS 456 clause 23.1.2 (L<sub>0</sub> = distance between points of zero moment, D<sub>f</sub> = slab thickness, b = actual width of an isolated flange):

answer: In addition, b<sub>f</sub> must not exceed b<sub>w</sub> plus half the clear distance to the adjacent beam on each side, and for an isolated beam it must not exceed the actual width.
L<sub>0</sub> for the continuous beam: the points of zero moment are roughly 0.15 of the span from each support, so L<sub>0</sub> ≈ 0.7 × 7500 = 5250 mm.

answer.text: Isolated T-beam with a 1200 mm flange:

answer: Comment: the isolated beam gets much less flange than its actual 1200 mm, because without slab on either side the flange is not held and shear lag is stronger. Using the whole slab width would overestimate the compression area and give an unsafe neutral axis and lever arm for deflection and crack checks.
Check: in each case the code formula, not the spacing limit, governed, as is usual for spans under about 10 m with beams 3 to 4 m apart.

bank.q: Explain the limit state of serviceability for deflection in IS 456: the limits, the span/effective depth method and the meaning of the modification factors. Check a simply supported T-beam of span 8 m with d = 450 mm, b<sub>w</sub> = 300 mm, b<sub>f</sub> = 1500 mm, p<sub>t</sub> = 0.30 % (on b<sub>f</sub> d) and f<sub>s</sub> = 230 N/mm².
outline: Service loads with load factor 1.0; short-term plus creep and shrinkage
Limits span/250 and span/350 or 20 mm
Basic L/d 7, 20, 26; 10/span over 10 m
k<sub>t</sub> from p<sub>t</sub> and f<sub>s</sub>; k<sub>c</sub> from p<sub>c</sub>; k<sub>f</sub> from b<sub>w</sub>/b<sub>f</sub>
Numbers: k<sub>t</sub> = 1.57, k<sub>f</sub> = 0.8, allowed 25.0 against 17.8
answer: Serviceability is checked under service loads, the characteristic loads with a partial safety factor of 1.0. Deflection has an immediate part, from the elastic and cracked stiffness of the beam, and a long-term part from creep under sustained load and from shrinkage, which together can be larger than the immediate part.

Limits (clause 23.2): the final deflection, including creep, shrinkage and temperature, measured from the as-cast level, must not exceed span/250; the deflection after partitions and finishes are built, including the creep and shrinkage after that time, must not exceed span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less.

Rather than computing these, IS 456 accepts a beam whose span/effective depth ratio is within L/d ≤ (L/d)basic × k<sub>t</sub> × k<sub>c</sub> × k<sub>f</sub>. The basic values are 7 for a cantilever, 20 for a simply supported span and 26 for a continuous span, for spans up to 10 m. For longer spans they are multiplied by 10/span; cantilevers longer than 10 m need a deflection calculation.

k<sub>t</sub> (Fig. 4) depends on the tension steel percentage p<sub>t</sub> and on the service steel stress f<sub>s</sub> = 0.58 f<sub>y</sub> × A<sub>st,req</sub>/A<sub>st,prov</sub>. A beam with little steel has a shallow cracked neutral axis and stays stiff, so k<sub>t</sub> reaches 2.0; k<sub>t</sub> falls as p<sub>t</sub> or f<sub>s</sub> grows. k<sub>c</sub> (Fig. 5) rewards compression steel, from 1.0 up to 1.5 at p<sub>c</sub> = 3 %, because compression steel resists creep. k<sub>f</sub> (Fig. 6) is applied to flanged beams: 0.8 when b<sub>w</sub>/b<sub>f</sub> ≤ 0.3, rising to 1.0 at b<sub>w</sub>/b<sub>f</sub> = 1; for such beams p<sub>t</sub> is worked out on b<sub>f</sub> d.

answer.pre:
actual L/d = 8000/450 = 17.8
(L/d)basic = 20 (simply supported, span < 10 m)
k<sub>t</sub> (p<sub>t</sub> = 0.30 %, f<sub>s</sub> = 230): 1/[0.225 + 0.00322 × 230 + 0.625 log₁₀ 0.30] = 1/0.639 = 1.57
k<sub>c</sub> = 1.0 (no compression steel)
b<sub>w</sub>/b<sub>f</sub> = 300/1500 = 0.20 ≤ 0.3  → k<sub>f</sub> = 0.80
allowed L/d = 20 × 1.57 × 1.0 × 0.80 = 25.0

answer: Since 17.8 < 25.0, the beam satisfies the deflection limits without a separate calculation.

Comment: k<sub>f</sub> below 1 reflects that a flanged section has much less concrete in the tension zone than a rectangle b<sub>f</sub> wide, so it is less stiff after cracking than its large p<sub>t</sub> base suggests. If the check had failed, the most effective remedy is more depth, which lowers L/d and f<sub>s</sub> together.
Check: without k<sub>f</sub> the allowed ratio would be 20 × 1.57 = 31.3; with k<sub>f</sub> it is 25.0, still 41 % above the actual 17.8 (25.0/17.8 = 1.41).

bank.q: A simply supported beam of effective span 6 m carries a dead load of 16 kN/m (self-weight included) and a live load of 12 kN/m. Its section is 300 mm × 550 mm with 30 mm clear cover and 8 mm stirrups. Using M20 and Fe415, design the tension steel, choose the bars, and check the code limits and the span/depth ratio.
outline: Factored load and moment
Effective depth from cover, stirrup and bar
M<sub>u,lim</sub> and the singly reinforced check
x<sub>u</sub>, lever arm and A<sub>st</sub>; Annex G check
Bar choice that keeps x<sub>u</sub> ≤ x<sub>u,max</sub>; spacing; min and max steel
Span/depth check with k<sub>t</sub>
answer: Effective depth, assuming 25 mm bars: d = 550 − 30 − 8 − 12.5 = 499.5 mm; take d = 500 mm.

Bar choice. The bars must give at least 1275.3 mm² but no more than A<sub>st,lim</sub> = 1435.8 mm², or the section becomes over-reinforced. 4 bars of 20 mm (1256.6 mm²) are too few. 3 bars of 25 mm (1472.6 mm²) are too many: x<sub>u</sub> = 361.05 × 1472.6/2160 = 246.2 mm > 240 mm. Provide 2 bars of 25 mm + 1 bar of 22 mm = 981.7 + 380.1 = 1361.9 mm².
Answer: 2 bars of 25 mm + 1 bar of 22 mm at the bottom (1362 mm²), with two 12 mm hanger bars at the top to hold the stirrups; shear stirrups are designed separately.
Check: the design moment 189.0 kN·m sits between the capacity of the bars provided (198.8 kN·m) and M<sub>u,lim</sub> (206.9 kN·m), and x<sub>u</sub>/d = 0.455 is below 0.48.

bank.q: A beam 300 mm wide must have an overall depth of 625 mm, giving d = 550 mm with bars in two layers, and d′ = 50 mm. It carries a factored moment of 450 kN·m. Using M20 and Fe415, design the compression and tension steel.
outline: M<sub>u,lim</sub> for the fixed section and the excess moment
ε<sub>sc</sub> at x<sub>u,max</sub> and f<sub>sc</sub> from the Fe415 curve (Table F)
A<sub>sc</sub>, A<sub>st2</sub>, A<sub>st,lim</sub> and the total A<sub>st</sub>
Bar choice and the 4 % limits
Check of the steel couple and of equilibrium

answer.text: Limiting moment of the fixed section:

answer: Bars: compression steel 4 bars of 20 mm (1256.6 mm²); tension steel 6 bars of 25 mm in two layers of three (2945.2 mm²), with a 25 mm spacer between layers. The centroid of the two layers is 30 + 8 + 25 + 12.5 = 75.5 mm above the soffit, so d = 625 − 75.5 = 549.5 mm, as assumed.

answer.pre:
0.04 b D = 0.04 × 300 × 625 = 7500 mm²; both 2945 and 1257 mm² are below it
minimum tension steel 0.85 × 300 × 550/415 = 338 mm²

answer.text: Equilibrium at x<sub>u</sub> = x<sub>u,max</sub> with the required areas:

answer: Comment: the compression steel is about 42 % of the tension steel here, because the moment is 80 % above M<sub>u,lim</sub>. If the depth could grow to about 815 mm (d ≈ 740 mm, from 0.138 × 20 × 300 × d² = 450 × 10⁶), M<sub>u,lim</sub> would reach 450 kN·m and no compression steel would be needed. The compression bars must be enclosed by stirrups to stop them buckling.

bank.q: An interior floor beam of a hall is simply supported over an effective span of 8 m; the beams are at 3.5 m centres, the slab is 120 mm thick, the web is 300 mm wide and the overall depth is 625 mm (d = 550 mm). It carries a factored moment of 550 kN·m. Using M20 and Fe415, find the effective flange width, locate the neutral axis and design the tension steel.
outline: b<sub>f</sub> from L<sub>0</sub>/6 + b<sub>w</sub> + 6Df and the spacing limit
Moment with the whole flange in compression
Neutral axis in the flange: rectangle b<sub>f</sub> wide
A<sub>st</sub>, bar choice in two layers, minimum steel on b<sub>w</sub> d
Checks of x<sub>u</sub>/d and of the moment

answer.text: Can the flange alone balance the moment?
answer.pre:
M<sub>f</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b<sub>f</sub> D<sub>f</sub> (d − 0.42 D<sub>f</sub>)
   = 0.36 × 20 × 2353 × 120 × (550 − 50.4)
   = 2 033 000 × 499.6 = 1015.7 kN·m
M<sub>u</sub> = 550 kN·m < 1015.7 kN·m → neutral axis inside the flange

answer.text: Design as a rectangle 2353 mm wide:

answer: Provide 6 bars of 25 mm (2945 mm²) in two layers of three; the centroid is 75.5 mm above the soffit, so d = 625 − 75.5 = 549.5 mm, as assumed. One layer of six bars would not fit in a 300 mm web.

answer.text: Check the moment with the bars provided:

answer: Comment: the neutral axis is only 62 mm deep because the 2.35 m wide slab supplies a huge compression area; the lever arm is 524 mm, 95 % of d. A rectangular beam 300 mm wide with the same d would have M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 20 × 300 × 550² = 250.5 kN·m, less than half the 550 kN·m this T-beam carries with tension steel only.

The deflection check would use p<sub>t</sub> = 100 × 2945/(2353 × 550) = 0.23 % and k<sub>f</sub> for b<sub>w</sub>/b<sub>f</sub> = 0.13 (0.8); over the supports of a continuous version the section would revert to a 300 mm rectangle.

bank.q: Find the moment of resistance of a T-beam with b<sub>f</sub> = 800 mm, D<sub>f</sub> = 100 mm, b<sub>w</sub> = 250 mm and d = 500 mm, reinforced with 5 bars of 25 mm. Use M20 and Fe415. Also find the limiting moment of the section.
outline: Tension force and the flange capacity: neutral axis in the web
First trial with y<sub>f</sub> = D<sub>f</sub> and the 3/7 x<sub>u</sub> test
Second solution with y<sub>f</sub> = 0.15 x<sub>u</sub> + 0.65 D<sub>f</sub>
Forces, arms and M<sub>u</sub>
M<sub>u,lim</sub> of the T-beam at x<sub>u,max</sub>

answer.pre:
A<sub>st</sub> = 5 × 490.9 = 2454.4 mm²
T = 0.87 × 415 × 2454.4 = 886.2 kN
flange alone at x<sub>u</sub> = D<sub>f</sub>: 0.36 × 20 × 800 × 100 = 576.0 kN < 886.2 kN → neutral axis in the web

answer.text: Trial with the whole slab at 0.45 f<sub>ck</sub>:
answer.pre:
0.36 × 20 × 250 x<sub>u</sub> + 0.45 × 20 × (800 − 250) × 100 = 886 150
1800 x<sub>u</sub> + 495 000 = 886 150  →  x<sub>u</sub> = 217.3 mm
3/7 × 217.3 = 93.1 mm < D<sub>f</sub> = 100 mm → the slab goes below the flat zone; use y<sub>f</sub>

1800 x<sub>u</sub> + 4950 × (0.15 x<sub>u</sub> + 65) = 886 150
1800 x<sub>u</sub> + 742.5 x<sub>u</sub> + 321 750 = 886 150  →  x<sub>u</sub> = 222.0 mm
y<sub>f</sub> = 0.15 × 222.0 + 65 = 98.3 mm  (≤ 100 mm)
x<sub>u,max</sub> = 0.48 × 500 = 240 mm → x<sub>u</sub> < x<sub>u,max</sub>, under-reinforced

answer.text: Limiting moment (x<sub>u</sub> = 240 mm; D<sub>f</sub> = 100 ≤ 3/7 × 240 = 102.9 mm, so y<sub>f</sub> = D<sub>f</sub>):

answer: Steel strain check: ε<sub>s</sub> = 0.0035 × (500 − 222.0)/222.0 = 0.0044 > 0.0038, so the bars have yielded as assumed.
Answer: M<sub>u</sub> = 381.9 kN·m, 97 % of the limiting moment 395.2 kN·m; the section is close to balanced.

Comment: treating it wrongly as a rectangle 800 mm wide would give x<sub>u</sub> = 886 150/(0.36 × 20 × 800) = 153.9 mm, a neutral axis outside the flange that the rectangle assumed, and an unsafe lever arm.

bank.q: Using the SP 16 design aids, find the reinforcement for a beam 300 mm wide with d = 450 mm and d′ = 50 mm in M25 and Fe415, for (a) M<sub>u</sub> = 180 kN·m and (b) M<sub>u</sub> = 250 kN·m. Show how the table values arise.
outline: M<sub>u</sub>/bd² against M<sub>u,lim</sub>/bd² = 3.45 N/mm²
(a) singly reinforced table: interpolate p<sub>t</sub>
(b) doubly reinforced tables: p<sub>c</sub> and p<sub>t</sub> at d′/d = 0.11
Formulas behind the tables
Bars and checks
answer: The flexure tables of SP 16 are the Annex G equations solved in advance: for a singly reinforced section p<sub>t</sub> = 50 (f<sub>ck</sub>/f<sub>y</sub>)[1 − √(1 − 4.6 (M<sub>u</sub>/bd²)/f<sub>ck</sub>)], listed against M<sub>u</sub>/bd² for each concrete grade (Tables 1 to 4) and steel grade (columns). The doubly reinforced Tables 45 to 56 list p<sub>t</sub> and p<sub>c</sub> against M<sub>u</sub>/bd² for d′/d = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15 and 0.20.
Provide 3 bars of 25 mm (1472.6 mm²). Check x<sub>u</sub> = 361.05 × 1472.6/(0.36 × 25 × 300) = 196.9 mm < x<sub>u,max</sub> = 216 mm.
Provide 3 bars of 12 mm at the top (339 mm²) and 4 bars of 25 mm at the bottom (1963.5 mm²).

Comment: the doubly reinforced tables have columns for d′/d = 0.10 and 0.15, so for 0.111 the designer interpolates between them; the formula above gives the value directly. Reading the Fe500 column by mistake in (a) would give p<sub>t</sub> = 0.814 %, about 17 % too little steel.

bank.q: A beam 300 mm × 500 mm has 3 bars of 16 mm at an effective depth of 450 mm, in M25 concrete. Taking E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√f<sub>ck</sub>, find the cracking moment from the transformed and from the gross section, the stresses just before cracking, and the concrete and steel stresses under a service moment of 55 kN·m.
outline: m = E<sub>s</sub>/E<sub>c</sub> and (m − 1)A<sub>st</sub>
Uncracked neutral axis and I
M<sub>cr</sub> = f<sub>cr</sub> I/y<sub>t</sub>; Annex C gross value
Stresses at first crack
Cracked section: x, I<sub>cr</sub>, f<sub>c</sub> and f<sub>s</sub> at 55 kN·m

answer.pre:
f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√25 = 3.5 N/mm²
M<sub>cr</sub> = 3.5 × 3289 × 10⁶ / 244.5 = 47.1 kN·m  (transformed)
M<sub>r</sub> = 3.5 × (300 × 500²/6) = 3.5 × 12.5 × 10⁶ = 43.75 kN·m  (gross, IS 456 Annex C)

top concrete: 47.1 × 10⁶ × 255.5 / (3289 × 10⁶) = 3.66 N/mm² compression
bottom concrete: 3.50 N/mm² tension (= f<sub>cr</sub>)
steel: m × 47.1 × 10⁶ × 194.5 / (3289 × 10⁶) = 22.3 N/mm²

answer: The steel stress at first cracking is only 22 N/mm², a twentieth of its yield: concrete cracks long before the steel does any real work.
Check by the lever arm: z = 450 − 105.3/3 = 414.9 mm; f<sub>s</sub> = M/(A<sub>st</sub> z) = 55 × 10⁶/(603.2 × 414.9) = 219.8 N/mm² ✓.

Comment: after cracking the second moment falls from 3289 × 10⁶ to 690 × 10⁶ mm⁴, a fifth, and the steel stress jumps from 22 to 220 N/mm². This is why deflection and crack width are computed on the cracked section, with I<sub>eff</sub> = I<sub>cr</sub>/[1.2 − (M<sub>r</sub>/M)(z/d)(1 − x/d)] = 1081 × 10⁶ mm⁴ for 55 kN·m.

bank.q: The beam designed in the singly reinforced question above (300 × 550 mm, d = 499.5 mm, 2 bars of 25 mm + 1 bar of 22 mm, M20, Fe415, 6 m span, 38 mm clear cover to the main bars) carries a service moment of 126 kN·m. Analyse its serviceability: span/depth, bar spacing and the crack width at the bottom corner (take m = 280/(3σcbc) = 13.33).
outline: Service moment is M<sub>u</sub>/1.5
Span/depth with k<sub>t</sub>
Bar spacing against Table 15
Cracked section: x, I<sub>cr</sub>, f<sub>s</sub>
Annex F: ε<sub>1</sub>, ε<sub>m</sub>, a<sub>cr</sub>, w<sub>cr</sub> against 0.3 mm and 0.2 mm
answer: The service moment is the factored moment divided by the load factor: 189.0/1.5 = 126 kN·m. Serviceability is checked at this moment, not at 189 kN·m.

Bar spacing: the clear gap between the bottom bars is (300 − 60 − 16 − 72)/2 = 76 mm, far below the Table 15 maximum of 180 mm for Fe415, so the detailing rule for crack control is met. The beam is 550 mm deep, less than 750 mm, so no side face steel is needed.

answer.text: Crack width at the corner bar (25 mm, centre 50.5 mm from side and soffit):

answer: Verdict: 0.17 mm is within the general limit of 0.3 mm and also within 0.2 mm, the limit for a member exposed to weather or moisture. The beam is serviceable on all three counts.

Comment: the concrete stress at service, 10.0 N/mm², is above the working stress permissible value σ<sub>cbc</sub> = 7 N/mm² for M20; that does not matter in limit state design, but it shows why the working stress method gives deeper beams. If the crack width had failed, the cheapest remedy is smaller bars at closer spacing (for example 4 bars of 22 mm), which reduces a<sub>cr</sub>.

bank.q: A contractor proposes to strengthen a 250 × 500 mm beam (d = 450 mm, M20, Fe415) by putting 4 bars of 25 mm in tension instead of a designed steel, arguing that more steel always means more strength. The beam must carry M<sub>u</sub> = 180 kN·m. Evaluate the proposal with IS 456 and recommend a better section.
outline: A<sub>st,lim</sub> and classification of 4 bars of 25 mm
Code moment of resistance M<sub>u,lim</sub> against 180 kN·m
True collapse moment by strain compatibility and the failure mode
Doubly reinforced alternative: A<sub>sc</sub>, A<sub>st</sub> and total steel
Recommendation
answer: The proposal: A<sub>st</sub> = 4 × 490.9 = 1963.5 mm², 82 % more than A<sub>st,lim</sub>. The estimate x<sub>u</sub> = 361.05 × 1963.5/(0.36 × 20 × 250) = 393.8 mm is far above 216 mm, so the section is over-reinforced.

Code verdict: IS 456 does not permit over-reinforced design; the moment of resistance credited to it is M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 139.7 kN·m, which is less than the 180 kN·m required. The proposal fails the code check however much steel is added.

answer.text: What actually happens (strain compatibility, Fe415 curve):

answer: So the beam would in fact just reach 180.9 kN·m, but the steel at failure is at 290.8 N/mm², below its design stress of 361 N/mm², and strained to only 0.00146. The concrete crushes before the steel yields: a sudden failure with no warning deflection. That is exactly the failure the code is written to prevent, and the 'more steel' argument is wrong: the 887 mm² above A<sub>st,lim</sub>, 45 % of the bars, adds nothing to the strength the code credits.

answer.text: Doubly reinforced alternative for 180 kN·m (d′ = 50 mm):

answer: A second alternative is a deeper beam: with D = 550 mm (d = 500 mm), M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 172.5 kN·m, still short of 180 kN·m, so a depth of about 560 mm would be needed for a singly reinforced section.

Recommendation: reject the proposal. Use the doubly reinforced section (2 bars of 16 mm at the top, 2 of 25 mm + 1 of 22 mm at the bottom), which carries 180 kN·m by the code, fails in a ductile way, and uses 16 % less steel than the over-reinforced scheme. If the headroom allows, a deeper singly reinforced beam is better still.

bank.q: A floor beam spanning 7 m (simply supported) must carry M<sub>u</sub> = 300 kN·m. The architect allows a web 300 mm wide and offers three schemes: (A) a 300 × 550 mm rectangle (d = 500 mm, d′ = 50 mm); (B) a deeper 300 × 600 mm rectangle (d = 550 mm); (C) scheme A cast with a 120 mm slab, giving b<sub>f</sub> = 1500 mm. Use M25 and Fe415. Design the steel for each, check deflection, and recommend one.
outline: M<sub>u,lim</sub> of A: doubly reinforced needed; A<sub>sc</sub> and A<sub>st</sub>
B: singly reinforced; A<sub>st</sub> and bar choice near x<sub>u,max</sub>
C: neutral axis in the flange; A<sub>st</sub>
Span/depth check of each with k<sub>t</sub>, k<sub>c</sub>, k<sub>f</sub>
Comparison of steel, concrete and margins; recommendation

answer.text: Scheme C, T-beam b<sub>f</sub> = 1500 mm, D<sub>f</sub> = 120 mm, d = 500 mm:

answer: All three pass the span/depth rule. A has the smallest margin relative to its L/d (20.6/14.0 = 1.47), C the largest (28.1/14.0 = 2.0).

head: Scheme
Steel needed (mm²)
Concrete in the web per metre (m³)
Remarks
rows: x<sub>u</sub> almost at x<sub>u,max</sub>, little ductility margin; 50 mm more headroom

answer: Evaluation: A works but needs the most steel, two layers of large bars and compression steel, because the moment is 16 % above its M<sub>u,lim</sub>. B removes the compression steel, but its neutral axis with the bars provided is 262.6 mm against a limit of 264 mm, so it is only just under-reinforced, and it costs 50 mm of headroom. C uses the slab that the floor needs anyway; the neutral axis is only 46 mm deep, the steel is the least, and the deflection margin is the largest.

Recommendation: scheme C, the T-beam, with 3 bars of 28 mm. It is valid only if the slab is cast monolithically with the beam and the beam is simply supported (sagging moment over the whole span); for a continuous beam the support sections would be rectangles 300 mm wide and would need their own check, where scheme A or B governs.
Check: in every scheme the steel provided gives at least 300 kN·m (A by the two-couple design, B: 361.05 × 1963.5 × (550 − 110.3) = 311.7 kN·m, C: 361.05 × 1847 × (500 − 0.42 × 49.4) = 319.6 kN·m).

glossary.def: Distance from the extreme compression fibre to the centroid of the tension steel.
The level of zero strain in a bent section; its depth from the top is x<sub>u</sub>.
The idealised shape of concrete stress at collapse, replaced by a force 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> at 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>.
The distance z between the compression and tension resultants, d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub> for a rectangular section.
x<sub>u,max</sub>, the deepest neutral axis that still lets the steel reach its limiting strain.
M<sub>u,lim</sub>, the largest moment a singly reinforced section may carry.
A section in which the steel reaches its limiting strain as the concrete reaches 0.0035.
A section with x<sub>u</sub> below x<sub>u,max</sub>; the steel yields first and the beam fails with warning.
A section with x<sub>u</sub> above x<sub>u,max</sub>; the concrete crushes first and the failure is sudden.
Bars near the compression face that carry part of the compression in a doubly reinforced beam.
Distance from the compression face to the centroid of the compression steel.
A high-strength deformed bar (Fe415, Fe500) whose design stress-strain curve bends gradually instead of yielding sharply.
The width of slab assumed to act with a T or L beam at a uniform stress.
The fall of compressive stress in a flange with distance from the web.
Points where the bending moment changes sign; their spacing L<sub>0</sub> sets the flange width of a continuous beam.
The Indian design aids for reinforced concrete to IS 456: tables and charts for flexure, compression and other actions.
The characteristic load with a load factor of 1.0, used for serviceability checks.
A factor (k<sub>t</sub>, k<sub>c</sub>, k<sub>f</sub>) that raises or lowers the basic span/depth ratio.
The slow growth of strain in concrete under a sustained stress.
The shortening of concrete as it dries, which also bends an unsymmetrically reinforced beam.
Longitudinal bars on the sides of beams deeper than 750 mm to control cracks there.
m, the ratio of the elastic modulus of steel to that of concrete.
A section in which steel is replaced by an equivalent area of concrete so one elastic analysis applies.
The moment at which the extreme tension fibre reaches the flexural tensile strength.
I<sub>eff</sub>, a stiffness between I<sub>cr</sub> and I<sub>gr</sub> that allows for concrete between cracks.
The stiffness added by uncracked concrete between flexural cracks.
